11702-washington-and-his-colleagues-a-ch:
Henry Jones Ford's 1918 chronicle, in the Chronicles of America series, follows Washington and his colleagues through the rise and fall of Federalism. Chapters cover an imitation court, great decisions, the master builder, and alarms and excursions.

Washington, glad to stay at Mount Vernon, was weary of public duties and reluctant to serve again, the book says. Later chapters take up tribute to the Algerines, French designs on America, a settlement with England, and party violence under John Adams. The volume is a textbook history of the early republic's first parties.
13618-the-cathedral-church-of-peterborou:
The Reverend W. D. Sweeting's guide to Peterborough Cathedral, first published in 1898 and reprinted in 1926 with fifty illustrations, describes the fabric of the church and gives a brief history of the episcopal see. It draws on Gunton's history, Dean Patrick's supplement, and other local authorities, and walks the reader through the building bay by bay.

Sweeting covers the famous west front, whose leaning stones worried engineers for years, the transepts, aisles, and chapels, and the restorations of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. He notes where old work was hacked away and where it survives. The book serves both visitors and students of English church architecture, pairing a clear ground plan of the stones with the story of the diocese.
14429-heroes-of-the-great-conflict-life-:
Major General James Harrison Wilson sketched the life of William Farrar Smith in this 1904 Wilmington volume, part of a series on heroes of the Civil War. Smith graduated from West Point in 1845 and served as a Union corps commander.

Wilson argues that official reports alone miss motives and character, so he fills in Smith's campaigns, his friction with senior officers, and his handling of his own division. The sketch covers the Peninsula and later service with frank judgments. It remains a useful short biography, written by a fellow general who knew the army's inner workings.
15560-young-folks-treasury-volume-3-of-1:
Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this third volume of the Young Folks' Treasury, published in New York in 1909 by the University Society, with Edward Everett Hale as associate editor. The volume, Classic Tales and Old-Fashioned Stories, draws on a large board of editors and advisers, including presidents Roosevelt and Cleveland, Cardinal Gibbons, and poet Bliss Carman.

Classic tales open the book: Don Quixote, adapted by John Lang, in seven parts from knighting and windmills to the knight of the white moon and Quixote's death. Gulliver's voyage to Lilliput follows, adapted for young readers. The treasury aims to give children great stories in clear, abridged form, with the authority of a national editorial board. It remains a window on Edwardian ideas of what children should read first.
22644-the-boy-scout-treasure-hunters-or-:
Charles Henry Lerrigo wrote The Boy Scout Treasure Hunters, or The Lost Treasure of Buffalo Hollow, a boys' novel published in 1917. Series books about Boy Scouts flooded the market in scouting's first decade, mixing outdoor craft with wholesome adventure. Lerrigo's troop hunts a lost treasure in a place called Buffalo Hollow.

The sample opens in a dining hall, where a lanky boy of fifteen or sixteen slips into a vacant seat just as the chaplain rises to say grace. After grace, loud talk is banned, though whispers pass if they stay quiet. Camp routine and boy fellowship frame the coming hunt. The book offers period scouting ideals, woodcraft, and a treasure plot built for young readers of its day.
24906-history-of-the-eighty-sixth-regime:
J. R. Kinnear of Cruger, Illinois, published this history of the Eighty-sixth Regiment, Illinois Volunteer Infantry, in Chicago in 1866. Written in part while the regiment still served, it won the approval of Colonel Fahnestock and his officers at Peoria before it went to press.

Kinnear tells the regiment's term of service in full. He notes that its story is also the story of its brigade brothers: the 85th, 125th, and 110th Illinois, with the 52nd Ohio and 22nd Indiana. Battle scenes show men falling like grass before the scythe under cross-fire, then falling back under cool, deliberate aim. The book stands as a soldier's own record of Civil War service.
2533-round-the-sofa:
Elizabeth Gaskell frames this book as a stay in Edinburgh, where a young woman lodges near her surgeon, Mr. Dawson, and spends long evenings with her governess. The house has a sofa at its heart, and around it the guests tell tales that fill the winter nights.

The stories range from a lady's strange fortunes to a tradesman turned farmer and a proud woman's hard lessons. Gaskell ties them together with the narrator's own voice, wry and warm. Readers get a set of linked tales that show her range, from ghostly hints to plain domestic comedy.
28634-religious-life-of-virginia-in-the-:
George MacLaren Brydon's Religious Life of Virginia in the Seventeenth Century, subtitled The Faith of Our Fathers, is Jamestown 350th Anniversary Booklet number 10, published in 1957. Brydon, historiographer of the Diocese of Virginia, traces a church carried across the Atlantic with common law and Parliament's enactments. Jamestown's men prayed daily at the setting of the watch, hoping their labor might convert the heathen.

The London Company organized its first settlement as a Church of England parish, with Richard Hakluyt, famed for travel books, as first rector in England. Robert Hunt came as vicar and pastor, and each new settlement became a parish with its rector. Four cities, modeled on Geneva, anchor the story: James City, Charles City, Henrico, and Elizabeth City.
29386-boys-and-girls-bookshelf-vol-2-of-:
Volume two of the seventeen-volume Boys and Girls Bookshelf, a plan of character building from the University Society, gathers folk lore, fables, and fairy tales for young readers. Its pages run from old fairy tales like Beauty and the Beast, Prince Darling, Rumpelstiltskin, and Rapunzel to short tales by Cecil Cavendish and others. The set as a whole spans fun, nature, songs, games, inventions, and famous men and women.

Each tale is short, clear, and meant to be read aloud or alone, with morals worn lightly. The book aims to shape character through wonder rather than lecture. Parents, teachers, and lovers of old children's books will find a rich, old-style sampler of the tales that shaped generations of young readers.
5870-hidden-treasure-the-story-of-a-chor:
Hidden Treasure tells how a chore boy made the old farm pay, opening with the old homestead, a day's work, and a rainy day. Chapters follow draining the pond, selling turtles, selling sand, a new aunt, the sale, power and banking, and running water. Tony, the dairy house, visitors, Ruth and the straw stack, new methods, and filling the incubator carry the farm story forward.

The book gives a practical farm tale for young people, where small enterprises and new implements turn a struggling place profitable. The chore boy's lessons are thrift, observation, and steady work, shown in deeds rather than lectures. The book suits young readers interested in farm life, and adults who enjoy old-fashioned stories of making a living from the land.
britannica-1911-alfalfa: Alfalfa, in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, is the American name for a leguminous plant, a member of the pulse family that fixes nitrogen in the soil. Its scientific name is Medicago sativa. Elsewhere the same plant is known as lucerne. The entry sends readers to the article under that name. That article gives the full account of the plant, its cultivation, and its use as fodder. The short notice fixes the two names as one plant, gives the botanical name, and points to where the detailed treatment stands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-farf:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Farfa describes a monastery about twenty-six miles from Rome, near the Farfa stream. Legend in the Chronicon Farfense credits the Syrian St. Laurentius with a first foundation. Archaeology suggests the earliest house rose on a pagan temple's ruins, and Vandals devastated it about 457.

In the seventh century monks from Gaul refounded Farfa about 681, heralding a Benedictine revival in Italy. The Constructio Monasterii Farfensis tells how Thomas of Maurienne, warned by a vision of Our Lady, restored the house with Duke Faroald's aid. Frankish abbots then ruled, and Farfa grew into Italy's most famed monastery after Nonantula, rich in churches and goldsmiths' work, before Saracens sacked it about 890.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jaffa:
Jaffa is a titular see in the Jerusalem patriarchate, and its city is very ancient. Before Joshua reached Palestine, Jaffa already appears on Karnak's pylons and Tell-el-Amarna's cuneiform tablets. Greek authors, following native legends, traced its founding to Jopes, daughter of Aeolus. They made it the scene of Andromeda's fable, exposed on a rock and rescued by Perseus. The tribe of Dan received Japho, or Jaffa, by allotment.

Yet Jaffa seems not to have belonged to the Jews before David conquered the maritime region. Under Solomon it served as landing port for cedars Hiram sent for Jerusalem's Temple. After Solomon's death it likely regained independence or fell to Israel's kings. The prophet Jonah took ship there for Tarshish. The entry follows a port where myth, scripture, and sea trade meet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-caraf:
Vincent Caraffa was the seventh Superior General of the Jesuits, born at Naples in 1585 and dying at Rome in 1649. Of the family of the Counts of Montorio and a relative of Paul IV, he entered the Society in 1604, taught philosophy, governed its principal Naples house. Was provincial when elected general at sixty, dying four years later.

Before his election he published, under the name Aloysius Sidereus, devotional works including Bundle of Myrrh in 1635. Way to Heaven, Citizen of Heaven, Pilgrim of Earth, Idea of the Christian Man, and The Seraph. His only known writing as general was an encyclical on preserving the Society's primitive spirit. His brief term coincided with Jansenism's opening war on the Jesuits, troubles with Palafox of Puebla, scandals in Spain and France. The martyrdoms of Jogues, Brébeuf, and others in Canada and England.
doe-osti-2585490-quantum-materials-for-n: Quantum materials for sensing and computing got their DOE report, and this text covers the fault-tolerant push. The pages detail the materials. The quantum engineers get their briefing. The materials were quantum. The push was fault-tolerant. The engineers got briefings.
doe-osti-2997203-net-zero-lime-kiln-and-: Net-zero lime kilns got their carbon removal, and this DOE report covers the facility design. The pages detail the approach. The cement folks get their roadmap. The kiln was net-zero lime. The facility was carbon removal. The folks were cement.
doe-osti-3001107-automation-of-debris-re: Debris removal got automated, and this DOE text resurfaces insulators in pulsed power. The pages detail the state-of-the-art findings. The engineers get their method. The systems were terawatt. The method was engineer. The findings were state-of-the-art.
doe-osti-3027643-identifying-opportuniti: Chemistry-quantum interfaces got opportunity-identified, and this DOE final reports the technical work. The pages detail the information findings. The chemists get their closeout. The science was quantum information. The closeout was chemist. The technical were report. The final were DOE.
doe-osti-3226168-one-earth-energy-co-sub: One Earth got FEED-studied, and this DOE text estimates Class 4 CO2 capture. The pages detail the facility findings. The energy folks get their data. The estimate was cost. The data were energy. The 2 were CO. The FEED were study.
doe-osti-3376003-automating-detection-an: PV plants got fault-automated, and this DOE text diagnoses underperformance. The pages detail the detection findings. The energy folks get their data. The failures were faults. The data were energy. The plants were PV. The underperformance were diagnosis. The faults were failures.
doe-osti-3893826-verification-and-valida: SEFOR got SFR-validated, and this DOE verification covers sodium fast reactor tools. The pages detail the verification findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The data was experimental. The data were nuclear. The SEFOR were tools. The experimental were data.
hidden-treasure-the-story-of-a-chore-boy:
Hidden Treasure, the story of a chore boy who made the old farm pay, by John Thomas Simpson, argues for farming as a boy's opportunity. Simpson's preface revisits the western Pennsylvania farm of his boyhood and finds a changed world: neighbors gone, names forgotten, fences broken, and the neat orchard gnarled and wild. Rich bottom land lies foul with rank growth, and the lane is too ruined for his automobile.

Philadelphia and London published the book in 1919, with a colored frontispiece and sixteen illustrations, as both story and lesson. Its chore boy takes such a run down place and finds the treasure of the title in soil, stock, and method rather than in any buried chest. Simpson wrote while rural districts were emptying into cities, and his tale answers with accounts: what drainage, rotation, and care can return to acres everyone else had written off.
nasa-tm-19670007345-imp-d-e-aimp-pfm-enc:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center issued this interface document, Revision A, in August 1966. It defines the pulse frequency modulation encoding system for the IMP D and IMP E satellites, part of the Interplanetary Monitoring Platform series. An interface document fixes exactly how separate pieces of hardware exchange signals, so experimenters and engineers build to the same rules.

Early sections spell out how the D and E encoding system differs from the one flown on IMP A, B, and C. The telemetry format and data processing rules follow, with four methods for reading out experiment digital words. Separate sections cover analog data, input characteristics, and calibration of the analog oscillator. Sync pulses supplied to experimenters are specified. The closing sections treat circuit design and fabrication, including an expanded evaluation of a MOSFET circuit approach.
nasa-tm-19720025112-drive-turbine-system:
Warren J. Whitney of the Lewis Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum in September 1972. It is part two of a study on drive turbines for turbofan simulators. A simulator is a test rig that spins a fan model so engineers can study it safely on the ground.

Whitney designs the core turbine that drives the rig fans. The fans came in one stage and two stage forms, with a wide span of pressure needs. His goal was one core turbine for all one stage fans. Paired with a duct turbine, it should also drive the two stage fans. One shared drive meant simpler, cheaper testing.
podcast-dannyjones-XG04I_vtQFA:
Kevin Knuth, a physicist who has worked with NASA, joins Danny Jones to talk about UFOs and trips to the Moon. The episode title says he comes clean on both topics. Knuth speaks from his work in physics and his study of strange craft reports.

Knuth gives his view on what the UFO reports may show and why the craft seem to break known rules. The talk then turns to why no crew has gone back to the Moon in decades. Jones asks the blunt questions that fans of the topic want asked. The library holds the talk as an archive record of the guest's stated views.
podcast-dannyjones-o4Xoh1sU7FA:
Writer Shane Cashman warns Danny Jones that Palantir and the DOGE project are building a terrifying surveillance system. Palantir, the data firm tied to intelligence agencies, builds tools that merge huge databases. Cashman argues those tools now reach deep into civilian government.

Cashman lays out how merged data on citizens could track nearly every move and purchase. He describes drones, cameras, and records feeding one all-seeing machine. Jones asks who watches the watchers and whether limits still exist. The watched, which may be everyone, get a plain case against the loss of privacy as we knew it.
podcast-joerogan-iOQdjgdRcfA:
Bret Weinstein is back with Rogan for episode 2198 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Weinstein, the biologist who co-hosts the DarkHorse podcast, returns to his standing themes: strange times, and institutions he says have been captured by the ideas they should test.

He gives Rogan his latest reading of science, media, and public health, in the long, careful sentences his fans know. Rogan, a friend, challenges him lightly and lets the case build. The episode is a dispatch for the heterodox, one more long entry in the record of a professor who left the classroom and kept teaching.
round-the-sofa:
Elizabeth Gaskell's Round the Sofa opens with a young narrator sent by her parents to Edinburgh for care under Mr. Dawson, a surgeon known for curing one class of diseases. She lodges with her governess near his house in the Old Town. Lessons from fine Edinburgh masters are to go with the medicines and exercises her health needs. At first the change feels dreary. She has left brothers, sisters, and a merry outdoor life at a country home for dull rooms and stiff street walks.

Evenings prove the worst in autumn, as they grow longer day by day. Money shapes the lodgings, since her parents are not rich, there are many children, and Mr. Dawson's care will cost a good deal. Her father, with no false shame, names the need for cheapness, and Dawson points them to rooms at No. 6 Cromer Street.
the-cathedral-church-of-peterborough-a-d:
The Rev. W. D. Sweeting, M.A., wrote this guide to Peterborough Cathedral, first published in February 1898. The London edition named here is a 1926 reprint from G. Bell and Sons, with fifty pictures. Its full title promises two things: an account of the building's fabric, and a brief history of the bishop's see.

Sweeting drew on earlier histories of the church, naming Gunton, Craddock, Paley, Poole, and Canon Davys among his sources. He also folded in a guide he had prepared in 1893, plus an account of the mosaic pavement in the choir. More than twenty years of living at Peterborough stand behind the book, and he notes points where his own study led him to differ from earlier writers.
washington-and-his-colleagues-a-chronicl: Henry Jones Ford wrote Washington and His Colleagues, a chronicle of the rise and fall of Federalism. Yale University Press issued it in 1918, in the Chronicles of America series. Pages present here hold the title page, contents, and the first lines of chapter one, so the history itself is barely begun. Contents promise an imitation court, great decisions, and the master builder. Tribute to the Algerines, French designs on America, and a settlement with England follow. Party violence and the personal rule of John Adams close the list.
young-folks-treasury-volume-3-of-12-clas: Hamilton Wright Mabie edited this twelve-volume Young Folks' Treasury, published in New York in 1909. Volume three covers classic tales and old-fashioned stories. Daniel Edwin Wheeler served as assistant editor for the volume. Pages present here hold title pages and staff lists, but no stories. The lists name Columbia president Nicholas Murray Butler among the advisers. The classic tales themselves stay absent from these pages, so their selection cannot be described here.
